Field surveys of White-spotted spinefoot (Siganus canaliculatus) in the coastal waters of the Indo-Pacific have provided detailed accounts of its life-history traits. Hatchlings emerge from fertilised eggs at an extremely modest size, with newly hatched larvae possessing a wet weight of just 0.00018 grams [Wwb = 0.00018 grams], a value that reflects the small diameter of the pelagic eggs. This initial mass is drastically lower than the ultimate wet weight attained by adults, which has been documented at 840 grams [Wwi = 840 grams] for the largest individuals in the population, a value consistent with the size range expected for a fast-growing tropical herbivore of this total length. This impressive growth trajectory from a lecithotrophic larva to a reproductively viable organism spans several orders of magnitude in body mass. Researchers have noted that males and females exhibit similar asymptotic sizes, with the maximum recorded total length reaching 40 centimeters [Li = 40 centimeters] in older specimens. Such a maximum length places Siganus canaliculatus among the larger members of its genus, a distinction that influences both its ecological role as a herbivore on seagrass beds and its vulnerability to fishing pressure across its range. The transition from a planktonic larva to a benthic juvenile marks a critical period of rapid mass gain and morphological transformation.

The onset of sexual maturation in White-spotted spinefoot has been characterised by examining gonadal development across multiple cohorts. Puberty is first observed once individuals attain a total length of 11.6 centimeters [Lp = 11.6 centimeters], a size that corresponds to a wet weight at puberty of approximately 21 grams [Wwp = approximately 21 grams]. This weight threshold is derived from the length-weight relationship typical of the species, and it marks the point at which vitellogenesis and spermiation commence. Reaching this size generally occurs within the first year of life under favourable conditions, although local variation in food availability can delay the process. At this stage, the fish undergo a pronounced allometric shift as resources are increasingly directed toward gonad maturation rather than solely toward somatic growth. The relatively early puberty, compared to some other siganids, allows the species to maintain high population turnover rates in the dynamic seagrass ecosystems it inhabits. Gravid individuals are commonly encountered during the warmer months, and spawning aggregations form near reef edges where gamete release occurs.

Reproductive output in White-spotted spinefoot has been studied extensively under controlled laboratory conditions to understand its fecundity schedule. At a stable water temperature of 28.3 °C [T = 28.3 °C], females exhibit a maximum daily egg production that equates to approximately 2740 eggs per spawning event [N_R_i = approximately 2740 eggs per spawning event] when spawning occurs on a daily basis, yielding 365 spawning events per year [F_R_i = 365 spawning events per year]. This extraordinarily high fecundity is typical of broadcast-spawning teleosts, where pelagic eggs face high mortality rates during the planktonic larval phase. The maximum reproductive rate is thus characterised by the combination of a very large clutch size and a compressed inter-spawning interval, allowing a single female to contribute millions of offspring to the larval pool over a single breeding season. This strategy is energetically demanding, and it is supported by the species' ability to continuously graze on abundant algal resources. Field observations confirm that spawning events are synchronised with lunar cycles, further optimising larval transport and survival.

Longevity records for Siganus canaliculatus indicate a maximum lifespan of approximately 3 years [am = approximately 3 years] when reared at a consistent environmental temperature of 28.3 °C [T = 28.3 °C]. This relatively short lifespan is characteristic of many fast-growing, high-fecundity tropical fish species that invest heavily in early reproduction rather than prolonged somatic maintenance. Mark-recapture studies have confirmed that very few individuals exceed this age in the wild, with senescence and natural mortality becoming evident after the second spawning season. The physiological deterioration associated with advanced age leads to reduced feeding efficiency and increased susceptibility to predation. Interestingly, the lifespan appears to be largely invariant across the species' geographic range, suggesting a genetically determined upper bound that is only minimally modulated by local environmental conditions. In contrast to longer-lived herbivorous fish, the white-spotted spinefoot completes its entire life cycle within a brief window, a pattern that aligns with its role as a highly productive component of tropical coastal food webs.

The timing of sexual maturation relative to ultimate size reveals that at a total length of 11.6 centimeters [Lp = 11.6 centimeters], individuals have achieved only about 29 percent of their maximal total length of 40 centimeters [Li = 40 centimeters]. This early maturation relative to ultimate size suggests that Siganus canaliculatus follows a strategy of rapid reproductive onset rather than delayed breeding. The corresponding wet weight at first spawning, recorded at 21 grams [Wwp = 21 grams], is similarly a small fraction of the maximum adult body mass of 840 grams [Wwi = 840 grams]. Such a large scope for growth after puberty allows individuals to continue increasing their fecundity with age, as larger, older females produce disproportionately more eggs. This pattern of early maturation with indeterminate growth is common among iteroparous tropical reef fish and ensures that even as annual survival declines with senescence, the population can be rapidly replenished by young, fecund recruits. The extreme r-selected strategy typical of broadcast-spawning teleosts is exemplified by the initial wet weight of 0.00018 grams [Wwb = 0.00018 grams], where a single reproductive event produces tens of thousands of offspring, each beginning life with minimal endogenous reserves.
